Graded ring S is Q[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=B+i for i=1..d
If d=0, interpret S as Q (no variables, hence no f_i witnesses needed)
Each f_i is homogeneous in S with weighted degree deg(f_i)=A+i
Regularity condition: in the successive quotient S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}), the class of f_i is not a zero-divisor (equivalently: (f_1,...,f_d) is a homogeneous regular sequence in S)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let A,B,d ∈ Z with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q_{A,B,d}(q)=∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) with Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1. If Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q], then in the weighted graded polynomial ring S=Q[x_1,...,x_d] (or S=Q if d=0) with deg(x_i)=B+i, there exist homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d ∈ S such that deg(f_i)=A+i for each i=1..d and for each i the class of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor (so f_1,...,f_d form a homogeneous regular sequence). Consequently, the graded data of S modulo this regular sequence yields the given expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) (as stated in the equivalence).

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
Let N(q):=prod_{i=1}^d (q^(A+i)-1) and D(q):=prod_{i=1}^d (q^(B+i)-1), with the empty product equal to 1 if d=0. Since (1-q^(A+i))/(1-q^(B+i))=(q^(A+i)-1)/(q^(B+i)-1) for each i, we have Q(q)=N(q)/D(q).

Because each factor q^(B+i)-1 is monic, D is monic. Hence Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if D divides N in Q[q]. Also, because D is monic, D divides N in Q[q] if and only if D divides N in C[q]: the forward implication is obvious; for the reverse one, if N=DP with P in C[q], divide N by D in Q[q] to get N=DS+R with S,R in Q[q] and either R=0 or deg R<deg D. Then R=D(P-S). If R were nonzero, deg R would be at least deg D, contradiction. So R=0 and N=DS with S in Q[q].

For a complex number alpha and a nonzero polynomial F, write m_alpha(F) for the multiplicity of alpha as a root of F, and set m_alpha(F)=0 when alpha is not a root. By factorization into linear factors over C, D divides N in C[q] if and only if m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C.

Now fix a positive integer n and choose a primitive n-th root of unity zeta in C. For any integer m>=1, zeta is a root of q^m-1 exactly when n divides m. Moreover, when n divides m, that root is simple, because the derivative of q^m-1 is m q^(m-1), and m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Therefore m_zeta(q^m-1)=1 if n|m, and m_zeta(q^m-1)=0 otherwise.

Summing over the factors in N and D gives m_zeta(N)=#{i in {1,...,d} : n divides A+i}=mu_n(A,d), and similarly m_zeta(D)=#{i in {1,...,d} : n divides B+i}=mu_n(B,d).

Suppose first that Q(q) belongs to Q[q]. Then D divides N in Q[q], hence also in C[q]. So m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C. Applying this to a primitive n-th root zeta, and using the displayed formulas, gives mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

Conversely, assume mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n. Let alpha be any complex number. If alpha is not a root of D, then m_alpha(D)=0 <= m_alpha(N). If alpha is a root of D, then alpha^(B+i)=1 for some i, so alpha is a root of unity. Let n be the order of alpha. Then alpha is a primitive n-th root of unity, so by the formulas above m_alpha(D)=mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d)=m_alpha(N). Thus m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C. Hence D divides N in C[q], and therefore also in Q[q]. Consequently Q(q)=N(q)/D(q) belongs to Q[q].

Thus Q(q) is in Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n, as claimed.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For fixed integers A,B,d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q(q) as the product over i from 1 to d of (1 minus q to the power A plus i) divided by (1 minus q to the power B plus i), with the convention that when d = 0 this product equals 1. Then Q(q) is a polynomial in the indeterminate q with rational coefficients (that is, Q(q) belongs to Q[q]) if and only if for every positive integer n, the number of indices i in {1,...,d} satisfying n divides B plus i is at most the number of indices i in {1,...,d} satisfying n divides A plus i.
quantifier_order: Fix integers A,B,d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0
Define Q(q) using a product over i from 1 to d, with empty product equal to 1 when d = 0
Define mu_n(C,d) for every positive integer n and every integer C as the count of i in {1,...,d} such that n divides C+i
Claim: Q(q) is in Q[q] if and only if for every positive integer n, mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d)

payload.statement_nl: Let A,B,d be integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 if d=0. For each positive integer n and each integer C, define mu_n(C,d) to be the number of indices i in {1,...,d} such that n divides C+i. Then Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

dependency_assessment.notes: No citations were invoked. The argument uses only elementary facts about polynomial division over Q and C, factorization over C, and root multiplicities of q^m-1.

result_payload.reason: The proof correctly establishes the equivalence by reducing polynomiality of Q(q)=N(q)/D(q) to divisibility D|N, then characterizing divisibility over C[q] via root multiplicities. For a primitive n-th root of unity, each factor q^m-1 contributes multiplicity exactly 1 iff n divides m, so the multiplicities of N and D at such roots are precisely mu_n(A,d) and mu_n(B,d). This gives both directions, including the converse for arbitrary roots of D by passing to their order. The empty-product case d=0 is also covered. No semantic drift or illegal dependency use is present.
